question: You are an orchestrator for a land-use digital twin. Use the dt4 forest biomass agent to answer: how much above-ground biomass does Kielder Forest hold in 2024 according to ESA Biomass CCI v7, with its uncertainty? Over the next 40 years, which management regime removes the most CO2 from the atmosphere for a typical Kielder stand, according to the yield-curve model and according to 3-PG? And which of the two growth models predicted the 2018-2024 CCI hold-out years better? Quote the numbers.

answer:
I ran three dt4 calls: `get_agb` for Kielder in 2024, `management_scenario` for Kielder over 40 years with both growth models and all four regimes, and `validate` for Kielder.

## 1. Kielder above-ground biomass in 2024 (ESA Biomass CCI v7, role: observed stock)

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean AGB | **116.8 Mg/ha** (± 18.0 Mg/ha SD of the area mean) |
| 90 % range of the mean | **87.3 – 146.3 Mg/ha** |
| Woodland area | 18,979 ha (33,969 pixels of 100 m) |
| Total AGB | **≈ 2.22 Mt dry matter** (2,216,622 Mg) |

That uncertainty is for the landscape mean. Single pixels vary much more: the average per-pixel SD is 59.6 Mg/ha, and 80 % of pixels fall between 35 and 178 Mg/ha. Scaling the 90 % range by the area gives a total of about **1.66 – 2.78 Mt**. That is my own multiplication, not a tool output.

## 2. Which regime removes the most CO2 over 40 years (2024–2064)

The model's "typical stand" is Sitka spruce, aged 50, starting at the 2024 CCI value of 116.8 Mg/ha. Negative numbers mean CO2 taken out of the atmosphere. Each figure is the cumulative net t CO2/ha with its 90 % range.

| Regime | Yield curve | 3-PG |
|---|---|---|
| Continuous cover | **−277.9** (−603.4 to −0.8) | −141.2 (−401.0 to +46.9) |
| No intervention | −239.3 (−342.3 to −138.8) | **−183.2** (−408.3 to −37.4) |
| Clearfell, no thinning | −114.2 (−368.0 to +104.9) | −86.4 (−346.3 to +142.6) |
| Thin and fell | −19.4 (−205.5 to +133.3) | −25.7 (−240.1 to +161.9) |

- **Yield-curve model: continuous cover is best**, at about −278 t CO2/ha, or −6.95 t CO2/ha/yr. It ends with 140.0 t C/ha, of which 22.1 t C/ha is in wood products.
- **3-PG: no intervention is best**, at about −183 t CO2/ha, or −4.58 t CO2/ha/yr. It ends with 129.0 t C/ha.

The two models disagree on the winner, and in both the top two regimes' 90 % ranges overlap a lot. The firm result is that both models agree on the bottom of the list. Under each model, the regimes that keep more standing biomass remove the most CO2, and the two clearfell regimes remove the least. Thin and fell removes almost nothing net over 40 years. These are management scenarios (role: response), not observations.

## 3. Which model predicted the 2018–2024 hold-out years better

Both models were fitted on CCI data for 2005–2017 and scored on 2018–2024. The score covers 13,972 pixel-years; 4 pixels felled in that period were left out.

| | RMSE | Bias | R² |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Yield curve** | **42.6 Mg/ha** | **+0.86** | **0.275** |
| 3-PG | 43.7 Mg/ha | +1.78 | 0.237 |

**The yield-curve model did better**, but only just, and neither model explains much of the pixel-to-pixel variation. Both match the landscape mean well up to 2022: observed 120.7 Mg/ha, yield curve 120.7, 3-PG 121.7. Neither picks up the CCI dip afterwards. In 2024 the observed mean is 117.7 Mg/ha, against 125.9 for the yield curve and 127.3 for 3-PG.

## Limits to keep in mind
- Both growth models were calibrated on CCI v7 alone, with no lidar or ground-plot data. The tool says radar saturation and thinning push the fitted productivity below Forest Research yield classes.
- The woodland area comes from a CCI-derived mask, not the National Forest Inventory map. The model assumes a single species, Sitka spruce.
- The 3-PG climate is an approximate long-term average typed in for Kielder, not gridded Met Office data.
